source: Orabona v10, section 4.2.1, Lemma 4.13, physical PDF page 52, printed page 40, first display and proof

slots.content: Finite horizon T with entries a_0,...,a_T >= 0. The offset a_0 is among these entries. The text states no strict positivity or lower bound on T.
f is non-increasing on its domain. Equality is permitted.
f is continuous on the stated domain, including its finite endpoint.
For round t=1,...,T the weight is a_t and the sample point is the current right endpoint a_0 + sum_{i=1}^t a_i. The proof writes this endpoint as s_t = sum_{i=0}^t a_i.
Integrate f(x) dx from a_0 to sum_{t=0}^T a_t. Both integration limits depend on the supplied data; s_0 = a_0 and s_T = sum_{t=0}^T a_t.
sum_{t=1}^T a_t f(a_0 + sum_{i=1}^t a_i) <= integral_{a_0}^{sum_{t=0}^T a_t} f(x) dx. This is an exact finite, one-sided inequality with coefficient 1.

proof_topology: Introduce s_t = sum_{i=0}^t a_i; s_t-s_{t-1}=a_t for t=1,...,T.
Identify the summand with a_t f(s_t), the integral of the constant f(s_t) on [s_{t-1},s_t].
Since s_{t-1} <= x <= s_t, non-increase gives f(s_t) <= f(x). Integrate this comparison on that interval.
Sum the per-interval inequalities. Additivity across adjacent intervals yields the integral on [s_0,s_T].
boundary_observations: a_0 can be zero and remains the lower integral endpoint. The sum of weighted samples starts at t=1.
Any later a_t=0 produces equal consecutive endpoints, zero rectangle and zero interval integral. For all later increments zero the two sides vanish.
T=0, if admitted by a formal horizon type, gives an empty sum and equal limits. The source does not single out this case.
The displayed lemma assumes continuity and nonnegative codomain even if one might prove variants with weaker conditions.
downstream: Printed pp.39-40 motivate the lemma by adaptive online subgradient descent (OSD). Equation (4.3) uses eta_t = D/sqrt(sum_{i=1}^t ||g_i||_2^2), skipping zero-gradient rounds.

Immediately after the proof, set a_t=||g_t||_2^2 for t>=1 as indicated by the displayed sum. The text uses f(x)=1/sqrt(x) and a_0 -> 0. The singularity at zero requires separate treatment; the function as written is outside the lemma's continuous domain at zero.

With the factor D/2 preceding the sum, the resulting upper bound is D sqrt(sum_{t=1}^T ||g_t||_2^2). This supplies the second term in the derivation leading to the (3/2)D sqrt(sum ||g_t||_2^2) regret bound (4.4).

Theorem 4.14, later on p.40, rescales the learning rates by sqrt(2)/2, skips zero-gradient updates, and states the improved D sqrt(2 sum ||g_t||_2^2) regret bound and a fixed-rate minimization expression. The lemma alone establishes the scalar sum-integral inequality.
